rich_summary: King Janamejaya asks the sage Vaisampayana to recount the origins and deeds of the Pandavas, who were said to be divine incarnations. The narrative begins with their father, King Pandu, hunting in the forest on the slopes of the Himalayas. Pandu shoots a pair of deer while they are mating, only to discover that the male deer is actually the sage Kindama disguised in animal form. Mortally wounded, the sage rebukes Pandu for killing a creature during intercourse, calling it cruel and unrighteous. In anger and grief, Kindama curses Pandu: whenever Pandu approaches a wife with sexual desire, he will die instantly. This curse becomes a pivotal turning point in the epic, explaining why the Pandavas will later be conceived through divine intervention rather than ordinary union.

highlight_spans.why: Janamejaya asks to hear the story of the Pandavas, framing the narrative shift toward their divine origins.
Pandu encounters and shoots the mating deer, the crucial act that triggers the tragic curse.
The wounded sage rebukes Pandu, introducing the moral argument about violence, timing, and dharma.
Kindama pronounces the devastating curse that Pandu will die the moment he approaches a wife with desire.

top_scenes.scene_text: In a dense Himalayan forest, King Pandu releases arrows at a pair of deer locked in mating, the golden‑feathered shafts striking them mid‑act.
The wounded deer transforms into the dying sage Kindama, lying on the forest floor while reproaching Pandu with grief and anger.
The sage raises himself in pain to pronounce a curse upon Pandu, the forest tense as the king realizes the fatal consequence of his act.
